Setter
SET-ter
n. (one who sets forth; in the phrase a setter forth of strange gods, a proclaimer of foreign deities)
Agent noun from set, Old English settan, to place. The phrase renders Greek katangeleus, a proclaimer or announcer, from katangello, to declare. The Athenian charge echoes the one brought against Socrates.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Paul's preaching in the Athenian market draws a technical accusation: “Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection” (Acts 17:18). A setter forth is a proclaimer, and the charge of introducing foreign deities was the same one on which Athens had condemned Socrates four centuries earlier. Luke tells us exactly what provoked it: Paul preached Jesus and the resurrection, and the hearers took Jesus and Anastasis for a pair of new divinities. Paul's answer on Mars' hill does not retreat but turns their own altar against them: “I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” (Acts 17:23). He is not setting forth a strange god but naming the God they had already confessed they did not know, and he ends where every true proclamation ends: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Acts 17:30).

Key Scripture

Act 17:18 — "Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him. And some said, What will this babbler say? other some, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods: because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection."

Act 17:23 — "For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you."

Act 17:30 — "And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:"

Modern Corruption

Paul's Athenian sermon is held up as a model of finding common ground with every religion, when its argument is that the God they confessed as unknown now commands all men everywhere to repent.

expand to see more

Acts 17 is the favourite text of religious pluralism and of a certain apologetic style that treats the sermon as a masterclass in affirming other faiths. On that reading Paul finds the Athenians already worshipping the true God under another name, quotes their poets approvingly, and declines to offend. The dictionary rejects it, because the sermon itself does not do what the reading requires.

Paul does begin from their altar and their poets; he is a missionary, not a boor, and starting where hearers stand is apostolic method. But he says they worship ignorantly, tells them God is not worshipped with men's hands, calls their images a product of ignorance that God had overlooked, commands repentance of all men everywhere, and announces a day of judgment by a Man whom God raised from the dead. Common ground was his starting point and never his conclusion. Some mocked, some delayed, and some believed — which is what preaching does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Agent noun from set; Greek katangeleus, a proclaimer; Acts 17:18 calls Paul a setter forth of strange gods.

Old English settan, to place, gives set and setter.

The phrase renders Greek katangeleus, a proclaimer or announcer.

Acts 17:18 is the only occurrence of setter in the Authorized Version.

The charge of introducing strange gods had condemned Socrates in Athens.

The hearers took Jesus and the resurrection for two new deities.
